title: Resistance: when cancer fights back
blurb: How cancer cells reroute around a blocked protein, and why combinations help.

steps.title: The drug worked... then it didn't

text.simple: Sometimes a drug shrinks a cancer, but months later it grows back. The cancer has become **resistant**.
text.student: **Drug resistance** is a major reason cancer treatments stop working. A few cells that survive the drug can multiply and take over. [@holohan2013]
text.deep: Resistance can be primary or acquired, arising through selection of pre-existing clones or adaptive (non-genetic) changes. [@holohan2013]

text.simple: The cancer can mutate its target protein so the drug's key no longer fits.
text.student: In some leukemia patients on imatinib, BCR-ABL1 picks up mutations in the drug pocket that stop imatinib from binding. [@gorre2001]
text.deep: Kinase-domain mutations (e.g., the T315I 'gatekeeper') or BCR-ABL1 amplification confer imatinib resistance, motivating second- and third-generation inhibitors. [@gorre2001]

text.simple: Signals in a cell travel along roads. If a drug blocks one road, the cancer can find a detour and keep the 'grow' signal going.
text.student: Blocking one protein in a pathway can release feedback brakes, so the signal comes back, or another pathway takes over (**bypass signaling**). [@lito2013]
text.deep: Relief of ERK-dependent negative feedback reactivates RTK/RAS signaling after BRAF inhibition; parallel PI3K/AKT activation provides bypass routes. [@lito2013]

try.note: A two-hit combo (◐ predicted by adding effects). Real combinations can be stronger or weaker than the sum.

text.simple: If you block two roads at the same time, it's much harder for the cancer to find a detour. That's why doctors often combine drugs.
text.student: Combination therapy hits several points at once. For example, BRAF + MEK inhibitors together worked better than BRAF alone in melanoma. [@flaherty2012]
text.deep: Vertical (same pathway) and horizontal (parallel pathway) combinations reduce escape routes; dabrafenib + trametinib improved progression-free survival over monotherapy. [@flaherty2012]

quiz.q: What does it mean when a cancer becomes 'resistant'?
options: The drug no longer works against it
quiz.explain: Resistance means the treatment stops working. [@holohan2013]

quiz.q: Which is a way cancer cells resist targeted drugs?
options: Mutating the drug's target so it no longer fits
quiz.explain: Target mutations like those in BCR-ABL1 can block drug binding. [@gorre2001]

options: They block several escape routes at once
quiz.explain: Hitting multiple points makes detours harder. [@flaherty2012]
